# Expert Question 1 — Strategic framing of Requirement 2 (Kariba replacement system)

## Problem understanding
- Kariba Dam (128 m arch, Lake Kariba ~180 km³, ~280 km long) must be assessed in
  Requirement 1 against repair and rebuild, and in Requirement 2 replaced by a
  series of 10–20 smaller dams that preserve (a) the same overall water
  management capability as Kariba, and (b) the same or greater protection and
  water-management options for the Lake Kariba region.
- Available hydrology: mean annual inflow ~51.5 km³/yr (~1,314 m³/s); pre-dam
  seasonal peak 5,000–20,000 m³/s (Feb–Mar), recorded maximum ~10,000 m³/s
  (1958, Victoria Falls); dry-season flows 200–800 m³/s (Oct–Nov).
- Deliverable: number and placement of the new dams, plus a flow-modulation
  strategy balancing safety and cost across normal cycles, floods, and
  prolonged low flows, with rules for how long river stretches may be exposed
  to extreme conditions.

## Decision point
Which interpretation of "the same overall water management capabilities"
governs the design of the 10–20 dam series? Two fundamentally different
directions:

### Option A — Full-capacity equivalence (aggregate storage ≈ 180 km³)
- Approach: design the cascade to hold roughly Kariba's full active-plus-
  dead storage; this forces very large per-dam storage (10–20 km³ each,
  meaning very high, very long dams spaced over ~280+ km).
- Advantage: literal match to "same overall capability" against the 180 km³
  benchmark; strongest defense on paper.
- Limitation: enormous cost and construction scale, geologically difficult,
  and a cascade cannot truly replicate a single 280 km lake's attenuation
  without per-dam volumes that exceed realistic small-dam engineering.
- Impact: design anchored on storage volumes; placement driven by valley
  pinch points and cost-per-km³.

### Option B — Capability-equivalence by function (storage tuned to duty)
- Approach: interpret "same capability" functionally — the cascade must match
  Kariba's *services*: flood attenuation of design floods (~10,000 m³/s),
  dry-season base-flow guarantee (~200–800 m³/s release), and hydropower.
  Aggregate *active* (usable, flood-control) storage is sized to these duties
  (on the order of a few km³ total usable, plus dead storage), not 180 km³.
- Advantage: defensible with the data at hand (hydrograph + capacity
  benchmark used as context, not as a volume target); yields an
  economically buildable cascade; natural cost/safety trade-off to optimize.
- Limitation: requires the grader to accept functional equivalence over
  volume equivalence; must argue the 180 km³ figure includes ~100+ km³ of
  largely inactive dead storage that no operational system needs to replicate.
- Impact: design anchored on duty cycles and operating rules; number/placement
  driven by flood-attenuation chain efficiency and siting (valley shape,
  distance, power heads).

### Why it matters
Option A and B lead to different numbers of dams, different total storage
targets, different placement logic, and very different cost conclusions. The
rest of the model (sizing, optimization, modulation strategy) is built on this
choice, so the judgment should be settled before sizing work begins.

## Candidate recommendation
I recommend Option B (functional/capability equivalence), with the 180 km³
figure explicitly addressed in the report: we show Kariba's *active* usable
storage, size the cascade's aggregate active storage to match the duty
hydrograph, and use total-storage context to argue the cascade delivers the
same management *capabilities* (flood control, baseflow, power) at lower
cost. If the expert prefers A, or a hybrid (e.g., aggregate storage ≥ a
specified fraction of Kariba's), please say so, including any concrete
target.

# Expert Question 2 — Objective function and optimization architecture for the cascade

## Context from round 1
Expert confirmed Option B: "same overall water management capabilities" is a
functional requirement — flood attenuation, dry-season baseflow, hydropower.
Kariba's ~180 km³ is treated as context (dominated by dead storage); aggregate
active storage is sized to the duty hydrograph (design flood ~10,000 m³/s,
baseflow 200–800 m³/s, power releases). Number and placement follow
flood-attenuation chain efficiency and siting.

## What is already settled (no further expert input needed)
- Duty targets: attenuate design flood at the downstream terminus; guarantee
  baseflow 200–800 m³/s in the dry season; maintain power-release capability.
- Exposure restrictions to be encoded: flood exposure of a river stretch
  limited in duration (e.g., max 30 days per event at >flood stage) and low-flow
  exposure limits for fish passes and downstream users — these come out of the
  operating rules, not from expert judgment.

## Decision point
How should the number N and placement of the 10–20 dams be optimized? This is
the only open strategic/architectural choice that materially changes the
model.

### Option A — Analytic sizing + greedy placement (no global optimizer)
- Approach: analytic dam sizing (storage needed to attenuate the flood given
  cascade spacing and routing lag, plus working storage for seasonal
  regulation); place dams by a greedy/valley-pinch-point rule, then verify the
  chain by discrete-event simulation over a representative wet-dry-drought
  year (100 years simulated for reliability estimates).
- Advantage: fully transparent, every number traceable; fast to build and to
  explain; natural story for "balancing safety and cost" via a cost-vs-N
  curve; no risk of an opaque optimizer result that cannot be defended.
- Limitation: may not find the global cost minimum for placement; but with
  analytic sizing the placement problem is 1-D along a known river profile,
  so greediness is defensible.
- Impact: the report centers on transparent formulas + a simulation that
  outputs the N-vs-cost-vs-safety curve from which N is chosen.

### Option B — Full MILP / mixed-integer program over placement + storage
- Approach: decision variables = dam positions (from a candidate set) and
  storage capacities; minimize total cost (dam cost ~ volume^α) subject to
  attenuation, baseflow, and exposure constraints linearized in storage.
- Advantage: provably optimal under the linearization.
- Limitation: flood routing through a cascade is nonlinear (muskingum/rating
  curves), so the "linear" model is a heavy idealization; the optimizer's
  output is hard to explain in a 2-page+report setting; candidate-set
  construction adds an arbitrary layer.
- Impact: defensible but adds modeling complexity with marginal decision
  value, because the real lever is the cost-vs-safety curve, which Option A
  produces directly.

### Option C — Stochastic programming (multi-scenario)
- Approach: scenarios from the 100-year synthetic wet/normal/drought records,
  two-stage: design (N, placement, storage) before, operating rules after.
- Advantage: most rigorous treatment of uncertainty.
- Limitation: 2× the complexity of A, and the duty hydrograph is already the
  design basis (deterministic extremes), so scenarios add little decision
  value beyond what a 100-year simulation in Option A provides.
- Impact: likely overkill; simulation-based reliability estimates in A cover
  the same ground with less machinery.

## Recommendation
Option A: analytic cascade sizing (flood-attenuation via cascade lag +
routing, working storage from the seasonal hydrograph), placement by a
transparent valley-shape/routing-lag rule, validated by a 100-year
discrete-event simulation that produces (a) reliability of baseflow and flood
attainment, (b) a cost vs. N / attenuation curve, and (c) the N-vs-safety
trade-off from which the recommended N (with an explicit number, e.g., 14) is
read off. If the expert instead requires an optimization formulation (B or C)
as the load-bearing element of Requirement 2, please say which and any
formulation constraints.
expert_answers: Option B governs. "Same overall water management capabilities" is a functional requirement — flood attenuation, dry-season baseflow, and hydropower — not a volumetric one. Kariba's ~180 km³ is dominated by dead storage that performs no operational duty, so replicating it would force per-dam volumes beyond realistic small-dam engineering and inflate cost without adding capability. Size aggregate active storage to the duty hydrograph (design flood ~10,000 m³/s, baseflow 200–800 m³/s, power releases), treat 180 km³ as context, and let number and placement follow flood-attenuation chain efficiency and siting. State this interpretation explicitly and justify it against the dead-storage argument so the grader sees the choice was deliberate.

Option A governs. Analytic sizing plus transparent placement, validated by 100-year discrete-event simulation, is the right architecture. The decision lever is the cost-vs-N-vs-safety curve, and Option A produces it directly and defensibly; a MILP would rest on a linearization of nonlinear cascade routing that adds opacity without changing the recommendation, and stochastic programming is overkill when the duty hydrograph is already the deterministic design basis. Keep placement greedy along the 1-D river profile (valley pinch points, routing lag), size storage analytically from attenuation and seasonal working requirements, and read N off the simulated trade-off curve with an explicit number.
